newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek Banks find derivatives tax bill ambiguous.
newsitem.headline: Greek Banks find derivatives tax bill ambiguous.

text.p: The Hellenic Bank Association (HBA) dismissed news reports it supported a planned 15 percent tax on derivatives and said a draft tax bill on derivatives was ambiguous and unlikely to help the market growth.

"The reported draft bill differs from the Hellenic Bank Association's proposals," said an HBA official. "It does not resolve taxation ambiguities with regard to derivatives trading and it is unlikely that it will help these markets grow in Greece."

Last July, the HBA submitted proposals on the derivatives market to both National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou and then Finance Minister Alexandros Papadopoulos, said the Hellenic Banks Associaition (HBA) in a statement.

The proposals were the outcome of a series of discussions between bank representatives and a consulting firm which prepared a study on relevant taxation issues in other OECD countries and the characteristics of Greece's taxation laws.
"Our proposals were in line with the experience in the majority of other countries," HBA said.
Its proposal underlined the need to resolve all taxation, accounting and legal issues concerning the derivatives market, it said.

These include a need for clarification on whether EFTE tax -- a special tax on bank activities -- would be imposed on derivatives and the characterisation of accrued gains or losses on these transactions as income from commercial activities, HBA said.
"For example a finance ministry circular issued in April 1 1994 has already stated that interest rate swaps are excluded from EFTE," HBA said.
Other clarification was necessary as regarded terms for the inclusion of derivatives either in the hedging book or trading book of banks.

HBA also said the accounting principles concerning the characterisation of these instruments had to be clarified as well as the required changes in Greek solvency law to allow domestic banks to sign ISDA (International Swap Dealers Association) agreements.
"The 15 percent tax on derivatives could be the coup-de-grace to a dying horse," said one market watcher.
Traders were also uncertain whether equity derivatives such as warrants issued by foreign securities firms would be encompassed by the measure.
"Derivatives transactions such as FRAs are also viewed as essential after Greece adopted the EU's capital adequacy directive (CAD)," said an HBA official, who requested anonymity.

"It states that banks and other financial institutions will face additional capital requirements if they fail to effectively hedge their positions," he said. --George Georgiopoulos, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
